Topic 3: Thermal Physics 3.1 Thermal Concepts Molecular theory of solids, liquids and gasses Solids: The molecules that make up a solid are arranged in regular repeating patterns. Low kinetic energy, particles are held firm but can vibrate. Liquid: Liquids possess more kinetic energy than solids and are held together by intermolecular forces. Because there is enough kinetic energy the particles are free to flow and assume shapes of containers. Gas: Gasses have high kinetic energy which creates less opportunities for molecules to interact and create intermolecular forces. The high kinetic energy makes particles fly and shoot everywhere. Plasma: At very high temperature atoms start to lose their electrons. The mixture of electrons and nuclei that result is the plasma. Temperature and absolute temperature Temperature is the measure of kinetic energy within a substance, temperature can describe how hot or cold an object is and determines the direction of heat flow. Thermal energy transfers from an object with higher temperature to another object with lower temperature. This transfer is called heat. Absolute zero: lowest possible temperature (0K -273.15 c) Internal Energy The internal energy of a substance is the sum of kinetic energy (thermal energy) and total potential energy (energy stored in bonds). Specific Heat Capacity A substance's heat capacity dictates the heat required to change the temperature of a substance. Option C: Optics C.1 Introduction to Imaging Real and Virtual Images Images formed by mirror and lenses can be categorized into real and virtual. Real Images can be projected and “touched”, formed by the intersection of real light rays. The real image of an erect object is always inverted. Virtual Images exist behind or “within” the mirror. Can not be “touched” and is the result of the intersection of virtual light rays. Mirrors Concave Mirror: A concave mirror has converging properties and will reflect light rays to the normal line. Key Rays: 1. Rays parallel to the principal axis will always converge into the focal point of a concave mirror. 2. Rays that are incident through the focal point will always reflect parallel to the principal axis. 3. Rays that are incident through the center of curvature will always be reflected directly back. 50

Convex Mirror: A convex mirror has diverging properties and will reflect light waves away from the normal. Key Rays 1. Rays parallel to the normal will always diverge away, producing a virtual ray that converges to the virtual focal point. 2. Rays that hit the virtual center of curvature will always reflect back and produce a virtual ray. Imaging When drawing the reflected image made by a mirror using a ray diagram, apply all important rays from the tip of the object. The intersection of all rays will be the reflected image. C.3 Fibre Optics Structure of Optic Fibres Optical fibers are made to have no light escape and chain instances of total internal inflection, this way the light rays can travel for very long instances while being orientated around obstacles. Structure: The interior of an optical fiber is glass and is surrounded by cladding which has a significantly higher refractive index. The cladding “traps” the light within the cable. Dispersion Dispersion is when the signals spread out as they travel along a fibre. Material Dispersion: As signals travel further and further the thousands of reflections can cause small splits in wavelength. This creates a delay and dispersion in the signal. Modal Dispersion or “WaveGuide Dispersion”: Is when multiple signals are sent across an optic fibre and are intentionally sent at different angles so multiple signals can be received. 58

Step-index Fibre: Step index fibres are used so that rays arrive at different times. Because rays are sent in at different incident angles, each ray has a different path length creating a change in the time it takes for each wave to travel. Graded Index Fibre: Graded index fibers are cables that allow for multiple waves to be sent and received at the same time. In the glass core of the cable the refractive index varies from highest at the center to the weakest at the ends. This creates many minute refractions until a critical angle is hit, and because waves travel at different speeds for each different path, they will all return at the end. Attenuation and the Decibel scale Another problem is that light signals scatter and the power/intensity of these waves decrease.
